title: Hamlet
author: William Shakespeare
edition: Standard Ebooks edition (modern text drawing on the 1604–05 Second Quarto and the 1623 First Folio)

sections.authorBiography: William Shakespeare was baptized in Stratford-upon-Avon on 26 April 1564, the son of John Shakespeare, a glover and town official, and Mary Arden. He probably attended Stratford's grammar school, married Anne Hathaway in 1582, and had three children: Susanna and the twins Hamnet and Judith (Hamnet died aged eleven in 1596). By the early 1590s he was an actor and playwright in London; from 1594 he was a sharer in the Lord Chamberlain's Men, who built the Globe theatre in 1599 and became the King's Men when James VI of Scotland became James I of England in 1603. He wrote or co-wrote about 38 plays and the Sonnets, and died in Stratford on 23 April 1616. Seven years later his fellow actors John Heminges and Henry Condell published 36 of his plays in the First Folio (1623).
sections.historicalContext: Hamlet was probably written between about 1599 and 1601, after Julius Caesar, for the Lord Chamberlain's Men at the Globe; Richard Burbage played the prince. Its story goes back to the Danish chronicle of Saxo Grammaticus (the tale of Amleth, written around 1200), retold in French by François de Belleforest (1570). An earlier English Hamlet play, now lost and often called the "Ur-Hamlet," was on stage by 1589, when Thomas Nashe joked about it. Revenge tragedy was a popular genre, following Thomas Kyd's The Spanish Tragedy (c. 1587). The play draws on live questions of its time: Protestant doubts about purgatory and ghosts (Hamlet studies at Wittenberg, Luther's university), the duty and danger of revenge, and succession, since Elizabeth I was old and had no heir.

publicationAndReception.publication: Hamlet survives in three early texts: a short First Quarto (1603), a long Second Quarto (1604–05) and the First Folio (1623), which differ in many lines and in whole passages. Modern editions, including the reading text here, combine them. It is Shakespeare's longest play.
publicationAndReception.then: It was popular at once: the Cambridge scholar Gabriel Harvey wrote in the margin of a book that it pleased "the wiser sort," and the First Quarto's title page says it had been acted in London and at Cambridge and Oxford. After 1660 it remained one of the most performed tragedies; the Romantic writers Goethe and Coleridge made Hamlet's divided mind the centre of interpretation.
publicationAndReception.now: Hamlet is perhaps the most performed and written-about play in the world. Readings have been psychological (Freud and Ernest Jones's Oedipal theory), political, feminist (Ophelia's madness and silencing) and existential. Films include Laurence Olivier's (1948), Grigori Kozintsev's (1964) and Kenneth Branagh's (1996); Disney's The Lion King (1994) borrows its plot. Lines such as "To be, or not to be" and "Something is rotten in the state of Denmark" are part of everyday English.

sections.overview: Prince Hamlet returns to Denmark for his father's funeral and finds his uncle Claudius on the throne, married to his mother Gertrude. Guards on the castle walls have seen a ghost that looks like the dead king. What the ghost tells Hamlet, and what Hamlet does and fails to do about it, is the play.

sections.whyItMatters: Hamlet is the great play about thinking: about how hard it is to know the truth, to act rightly when you are unsure, and to live with grief, anger and doubt. Its questions about revenge, mental health, family loyalty and political corruption remain urgent, and its language is the most quoted in English.

spoilerOverview.text: The Ghost says Claudius murdered him and demands revenge. Hamlet feigns madness, rejects Ophelia, and stages a play (The Mousetrap) that confirms Claudius's guilt. He spares Claudius at prayer, then kills Polonius, hidden behind a curtain, by mistake. Claudius sends Hamlet to England to be executed; Hamlet escapes, sending Rosencrantz and Guildenstern to their deaths. Ophelia goes mad and drowns. Laertes returns for revenge, and Claudius plots a rigged fencing match with a poisoned blade and poisoned wine. Gertrude drinks the poison; Laertes and Hamlet are both wounded with the poisoned blade; Hamlet kills Claudius and dies in Horatio's arms. Fortinbras of Norway takes the throne.

segments.script: What the book is about (no spoilers): Prince Hamlet returns to Denmark for his father's funeral and finds his uncle Claudius on the throne, married to his mother Gertrude. Guards on the castle walls have seen a ghost that looks like the dead king. What the ghost tells Hamlet, and what Hamlet does and fails to do about it, is the play. Themes to track: revenge and justice: the Ghost demands revenge; is it a duty, a crime or both? action and delay: why does Hamlet wait? Thought, conscience, doubt, or circumstance? appearance and reality: "seems" versus "is"; feigned madness, spying and plays within plays. death and mortality: from the Ghost to the gravediggers, what death means and what it makes of us. corruption and the state: "Something is rotten in the state of Denmark."

strategies.label: Wait time
strategies.howTo: Pause at least 3 seconds after asking (5 to 10 for DOK 3 and 4 questions) before calling on anyone, and pause again after a student answers so others can add on. Call on students at random, not only volunteers.

strategies.label: Think-pair-share
strategies.howTo: One minute of silent thinking or jotting, two minutes with a partner, then pairs report. Use it for every DOK 3 and 4 question so all students rehearse an answer.

strategies.label: Follow-up probes
strategies.howTo: Answer a response with a probe instead of a verdict: ask for the line that proves it, ask "why?" or "how do you know?", or ask another student to agree, extend or challenge.

strategies.label: Student-generated questions
strategies.howTo: Students write their own questions at each level (a recall, a "why/how" and a "should/what if" question), trade them, and answer a classmate's. The teacher picks one or two for the whole class.

strategies.label: Turn and talk
strategies.howTo: A 60-second partner check for literal questions, so every student says the answer aloud before one is called on.

strategies.label: Cold call with support
strategies.howTo: Call on a student by name after the wait time; if they are stuck, offer a choice of two answers or let them "phone a friend" and come back to them.

strategies.label: Socratic circle
strategies.howTo: Inner circle discusses for 5 minutes while the outer circle tracks evidence and questions; then swap.

strategies.label: Four corners / take a stand
strategies.howTo: Students move to Agree / Somewhat agree / Somewhat disagree / Disagree and must cite a line to defend the position; anyone may move after hearing evidence.

literal.label: Literal / recall
literal.scaffold: Sentence starter: “In this scene, … because the text says …”
literal.extension: Note how this detail is set up or echoed elsewhere in Hamlet.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?

inferential.label: Inferential / analytical
inferential.scaffold: Sentence starter: “The text says …, which suggests … because …”
inferential.extension: Test your reading against one critical approach (formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist) and say what it adds.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?

evaluative.label: Evaluative / synthesis / creative
evaluative.scaffold: Sentence starter: “I (dis)agree that … because …; someone might object that …, but …”
evaluative.extension: Situate your judgment in a critical conversation about Hamlet: whose reading does yours support or challenge?
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

questioning.alignment: Questioning design (our description; see docs/questioning-alignment.md): every lesson offers questions at three cognitive levels with DOK tags, built-in wait time, follow-up probes after each answer, think-pair-share for higher-order items and a student-generated question routine, with a level-specific focus set for each of the eleven rigor levels. It is designed to support classroom observation frameworks such as the NIET Teaching Standards Rubric (Questioning indicator); it is not NIET material and is not endorsed by NIET.

Where does the scene take place?

shortAnswer: Explain how revenge and justice develops from the beginning of the play to the end. Use two scenes.
Explain how action and delay develops from the beginning of the play to the end. Use two scenes.
Explain how appearance and reality develops from the beginning of the play to the end. Use two scenes.
wholeBookTest.essay: Choose one of the play's central concerns (revenge and justice, action and delay, appearance and reality, death and mortality, corruption and the state) and argue how the ending reframes it.

middleSchool.label: Middle School
middleSchool.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track): write a five-paragraph essay explaining what Hamlet teaches about revenge and justice. Use at least three quotations from passages your teacher selects from different parts of the book.

hsFreshman.label: HS Freshman
hsFreshman.text: Write a multi-paragraph essay explaining how William Shakespeare develops revenge and justice in Hamlet. Use evidence from the beginning, middle and end of the book.

hsSophomore.label: HS Sophomore
hsSophomore.text: Write an argumentative essay analyzing how William Shakespeare develops revenge and justice across Hamlet. Trace the idea through at least three scenes and address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.label: HS Junior
hsJunior.text: Write an analytical essay on how the structure of Hamlet (its order, turns and ending) shapes the meaning of revenge and justice. Discuss at least one place where the book leaves the question open.

hsSenior.label: HS Senior
hsSenior.text: Write a sustained argument comparing two interpretations of revenge and justice in Hamlet. Weigh the evidence for each and defend the stronger reading in a mature, well-organized essay.

ap.label: AP
ap.text: Write a literary argument: develop a defensible thesis about how William Shakespeare's choices in Hamlet (a recurring element, structure and narration) shape a complex understanding of revenge and justice, weigh at least one competing reading, and sustain commentary on well-chosen evidence. Do not merely summarize.

collegeFreshman.label: College Freshman
collegeFreshman.text: Write a researched essay (4–6 pages) that places Hamlet's treatment of revenge and justice in its historical context, using at least two scholarly sources.

collegeSophomore.label: College Sophomore
collegeSophomore.text: Write a contextual essay (6–8 pages) on revenge and justice in Hamlet that reads the play against its genre and period and engages two published critics. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeJunior.label: College Junior
collegeJunior.text: Write a theoretically informed essay (8–10 pages) on revenge and justice in Hamlet. Name your critical method, apply it closely, and acknowledge its limits. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeSenior.label: College Senior
collegeSenior.text: Write a research paper (12–15 pages) with an original argument about revenge and justice in Hamlet, engaging at least four scholarly sources in Chicago style. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

graduate.label: Graduate / PhD
graduate.text: Write a seminar paper (15–20 pages) that intervenes in the critical conversation on revenge and justice in Hamlet, engaging the relevant scholarship and textual history. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

hsFreshman.text: Write a multi-paragraph essay explaining how William Shakespeare develops appearance and reality in Hamlet. Use evidence from the beginning, middle and end of the book.

hsSophomore.label: HS Sophomore
hsSophomore.text: Write an argumentative essay analyzing how William Shakespeare develops appearance and reality across Hamlet. Trace the idea through at least three scenes and address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.label: HS Junior
hsJunior.text: Write an analytical essay on how the structure of Hamlet (its order, turns and ending) shapes the meaning of appearance and reality. Discuss at least one place where the book leaves the question open.

hsSenior.label: HS Senior
hsSenior.text: Write a sustained argument comparing two interpretations of appearance and reality in Hamlet. Weigh the evidence for each and defend the stronger reading in a mature, well-organized essay.

ap.label: AP
ap.text: Write a literary argument: develop a defensible thesis about how William Shakespeare's choices in Hamlet (a recurring element, structure and narration) shape a complex understanding of appearance and reality, weigh at least one competing reading, and sustain commentary on well-chosen evidence. Do not merely summarize.

collegeFreshman.label: College Freshman
collegeFreshman.text: Write a researched essay (4–6 pages) that places Hamlet's treatment of appearance and reality in its historical context, using at least two scholarly sources.

collegeSophomore.label: College Sophomore
collegeSophomore.text: Write a contextual essay (6–8 pages) on appearance and reality in Hamlet that reads the play against its genre and period and engages two published critics. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeJunior.label: College Junior
collegeJunior.text: Write a theoretically informed essay (8–10 pages) on appearance and reality in Hamlet. Name your critical method, apply it closely, and acknowledge its limits. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

collegeSenior.label: College Senior
collegeSenior.text: Write a research paper (12–15 pages) with an original argument about appearance and reality in Hamlet, engaging at least four scholarly sources in Chicago style. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

graduate.label: Graduate / PhD
graduate.text: Write a seminar paper (15–20 pages) that intervenes in the critical conversation on appearance and reality in Hamlet, engaging the relevant scholarship and textual history. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.
